extracted.intended_audience: aspiring poets, translators, and literary students / critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for composing, translating, and judging poetry (and some prose diction) — covering idiomatic translation, poetic diction, taste formation, and pedagogy of reading aloud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn vocabulary with objects & native contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn all the words with the objects before you, and without the intermediation of the English terms; accompany native speakers and call every thing by its native name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice by walking with native speakers through everyday places (gardens, farmyard, market), use advertisements, farces, jest books, and children's conversation to gain a home-like acquaintance with the language rather than relying only on polite literature or society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate from living speech (Luther's injunction)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Denn man muss ... die Mutter in Hause, die Kinder auf den Gassen, den gemeinen Mann auf dem Markte … fragen: und denselbigen auf das Maul sehen wie sie reden, und darnach dolmetschen.” — i.e. translate according to how common people actually speak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe idiomatic usage and the mouths of speakers; render speech as it is used by mothers, children, and market‑people so that readers recognize living speech and feel you 'talk German with them.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious poetry: pair natural images with elevated mysterious feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: When feelings are 'wrought above the natural pitch by the belief of something mysterious, while all the images are purely natural,' religion and poetry strike deepest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use purely natural imagery but intensify feeling via belief in mystery; the combination produces the deepest religious poetic effect (example lines from Ottfried describing infancy of Christ).

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow thoughts to mature (avoid premature/immoderate authorship)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘With the greatest possible solicitude avoid authorship. Too early or immoderately employed, it makes the head waste and the heart empty; ... he who sends away through the pen and the press every thought, the moment it occurs to him, will in a short time have sent all away.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not publish every passing thought. Like physiological secretions, thoughts must be 'taken up again into the circulation' and re‑secreted to ensure intellectual vigour; let ideas mature before committing them to print.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete adequateness of manner to matter ('satisfying entireness')
rubrics_metrics.description: Poems that possess 'that satisfying entireness, that complete adequateness of the manner to the matter' (as in Anacreon and Catullus) are most pleasing: the manner must suit the material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a unity where style and subject are perfectly matched; strive for spontaneous energy rather than mere artifice, and value a polished adequacy of form to content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquire good taste by studying the best models (defer to matured reputation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good taste must be acquired, and like all other good things, is the result of thought and the submissive study of the best models; presume those to be the best whose reputation 'has been matured into fame by the consent of ages.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study canonical authorities (e.g., Sir J. Reynolds, Harris of Salisbury) and the classics; cultivate taste through disciplined reading of time‑tested works rather than following ephemeral fashions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect differences in poetic idiom across languages
rubrics_metrics.description: The language of poetry is more distinct from that of prose in Italian (and Greek) than in English; English 'demands a denser body of thought as the condition of a high polish' and the genius of languages differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful that what works in one language may not in another; the translator and poet must account for structural and idiomatic differences when rendering style or form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about translating foreign poetic excellence into English
rubrics_metrics.description: Translation may be discouraged by the 'different genius of the English mind and language' — even where the original possesses satisfying qualities, English may require a different density of thought and idiom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid literal or presumptuous renderings; consider whether a faithful translation can preserve the original's perfection given language‑specific poetic idioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different modes for reading vs speaking (pedagogy of oral reading)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an error in teachers to enforce the necessity of reading as they would talk — reciting another's written thoughts and uttering one's own momentary thoughts are widely different acts requiring different enunciation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not force children to 'read as they speak'; pedagogical devices that try to mimic conversational ease (e.g., processions and public confessions) can have harmful moral and expressive effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against prose‑like diction in poetry except by voice justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Though some passages approximate prose, the preface's theory defends guarding against an approximation of prose in poetry; where prose-like phrasing occurs, it must be justified (e.g., by the narrator's persona).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain poetic diction and avoid prose structures unless the narrative voice or dramatic purpose explicitly allows conversational phrasing (Wordsworth's selective uses are noted as exceptions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve precise historical/theatrical senses of words (avoid equivocation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Object to any extension of the meaning of 'scene' beyond its theatrical reference; the word can signify scenery or the characters/actions on stage, and broadening its sense increases equivocation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep original significations full in mind to prevent obscurity; prefer precise, historically grounded meanings to vague modern extensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value compound and untranslatable epithets (beware loss in translation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain compound epithets (e.g., German compound epithets) may be 'untranslatable' and convey force and felicity not easily rendered into English; the German's facility with compounds approaches the Greek in force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When translating or emulating such epithet use, recognize potential loss; seek equivalents that preserve force and intimacy rather than literal words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic quality: flow and tender enthusiasm
rubrics_metrics.description: Passages possessing 'a flow, and a tender enthusiasm' are of considerable poetic merit and will interest the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for smoothness of movement and sincere feeling; the interplay of genuine emotion and well-modulated phrasing produces engaging poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer spontaneous-appearing composition to over-laboured effort
rubrics_metrics.description: Works that read as though 'elaborated with great care' yet refer to 'a spontaneous energy rather than to voluntary effort' are prized; the appearance of spontaneity enhances poetic charm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate craft until artifice disappears; the best small poems can be carefully made yet feel naturally arising from feeling and habit.
